sections.title: What makes a rule a function?
sections.label: Classify
sections.intro: Read the inputs first. A function assigns exactly one output to every permitted input.

blocks.html: Two arrows may arrive at one output. Two different outputs from a single input break the function rule.

blocks.prompt:
The table shows a relation from the input values to the output values.

InputOutput
\(4\)\(-1\)
\(9\)\(9\)
\(4\)\(14\)

Which description fits this rule?

options.C: A relation that is not a function

blocks.solution:
Check how many outputs belong to each input first, then look for shared outputs.

The input \(4\) has the two different outputs \(-1\) and \(14\).

Final answer: A relation that is not a function.
blocks.hint: Check how many outputs belong to each input first, then look for shared outputs.

sections.title: How do I use function notation?
sections.label: Values
sections.intro: Read the bracket as an instruction about the input. Replace the input wherever it occurs in the rule.

blocks.html: \(f(3)\) means apply the rule at input \(3\).

blocks.prompt:
A function is defined by \(f:x\mapsto 3 \left(x - 5\right)^{2}\) for all real \(x\).

Find \(f(4)\).
blocks.solution:

Subtract \(5\) within the brackets before squaring, then multiply and add.

Final answer: \(3\).
blocks.hint: Replace every occurrence of the input by the named value.

blocks.html: Do not multiply the name of the function by its input.

sections.title: When is a function one-to-one?
sections.label: One to one
sections.intro: Compare outputs for different inputs. If at least two distinct inputs give the same output, it is many-to-one.

blocks.html: A one-to-one function has one input for each output in its range.

Which description fits this rule?

blocks.solution:

Every listed input has exactly one output. The first and last inputs both give \(3\).

Final answer: A many-to-one function.

sections.title: Which inputs make a real square root?
sections.label: Radicand
sections.intro: Locate the expression underneath the root sign. Its value must be at least zero.

blocks.html: Include the zero endpoint of a square root when nothing else excludes it.

figure.alt: The square-root curve starts at one point and goes right and up.
figure.caption: The square-root curve starts at one point and goes right and up.

blocks.prompt:
Consider the real-valued function \(f(x)=\sqrt{4 x - 16} + 3\) on its largest possible real domain.

State the domain of the function.
blocks.solution:
Make the expression inside the square root non-negative.

The radicand is zero at the left endpoint, so the endpoint is included.

Final answer: \(x\ge 4\).
blocks.hint: Make the expression inside the square root non-negative.

retry.feedback: The radicand is zero at the left endpoint, so the endpoint is included.

blocks.html: A square root can equal zero. Use a closed endpoint in this case.

sections.title: What changes when a square root is subtracted?
sections.label: Outputs
sections.intro: Track how its input changes from zero to large positive values. Multiplying a result by a negative number reverses its order.

blocks.html: A square-root term subtracted from a constant gives a maximum output at the start of the domain.

blocks.prompt:

Find the range of the function.
blocks.solution:
Use the limiting or extreme values of the output.

Subtracting a non-negative square-root value from \(0\) gives a maximum of \(0\).

Final answer: \(y\le 0\).
blocks.hint: Use the limiting or extreme values of the output.

blocks.html: The minimum input need not give the minimum output.

blocks.prompt:

Final answer: \(y\le 1\).
blocks.hint: Use the limiting or extreme values of the output.

sections.title: Which input and output are missing from a reciprocal?
sections.label: Fractions
sections.intro: Check where the denominator is zero. Then ask which horizontal level the output approaches without reaching.

blocks.html: A non-zero constant divided by a finite non-zero number never equals zero.

Find the range of the function.

The fraction cannot equal zero. Solving \(y=-3 + \frac{2}{x - 6}\) for \(x\) gives a real input for every \(y\ne -3\) .

Final answer: \(y\ne -3\).

addmaths-0606-functions-composites.description: Choose the right order, apply the inner rule and restrict its output when needed.

sections.title: Which rule goes first?
sections.label: Order
sections.intro: Think of two boxes connected in a row. The inner rule sees the original input. Its result is what enters the outer rule.

blocks.html: \(fg(x)=f(g(x))\). Work from the bracket outwards.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=3 x + 5\) and \(g(x)=\left(x - 4\right)^{2}\).

Find an expression for \(fg(x)\).
blocks.solution:
Apply the right-hand function first.

Substitute \(\left(x - 4\right)^{2}\) for the input of \(f\), then simplify.

Final answer: \(3 x^{2} - 24 x + 53\).
blocks.hint: Apply the right-hand function first.

retry.feedback: This applies the functions in the opposite order.

blocks.html: Interchanging the two rules can give a different output.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=4 x + 5\) and \(g(x)=\left(x - 5\right)^{2}\).

Find an expression for \(fg(x)\).
blocks.solution:
Apply the right-hand function first.

Substitute \(\left(x - 5\right)^{2}\) for the input of \(f\), then simplify.

Final answer: \(4 x^{2} - 40 x + 105\).
blocks.hint: Apply the right-hand function first.

retry.feedback: This applies the functions in the opposite order.

sections.title: Does f squared mean the output is squared?
sections.label: Repeat
sections.intro: In the Cambridge composition notation the superscript on the function name indicates that the rule is applied twice.

blocks.html: \(f^2(x)=f(f(x))\) in this context.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=4 x + 6\) and \(g(x)=\left(x - 3\right)^{2}\).

Find \(f^2(x)\), where the superscript denotes composition.

field.label: Expression for f composed with itself

blocks.solution:
Use the output of the first application of f as a new input.

Substitute \(4 x + 6\) for x in \(f(x)\).

Final answer: \(16 x + 30\).
blocks.hint: Use the output of the first application of f as a new input.

retry.feedback: Composition applies the function again. Squaring the output gives a different expression.

blocks.html: Applying the same function twice is different from squaring a value.

blocks.prompt:

Find \(f^2(x)\), where the superscript denotes composition.

field.label: Expression for f composed with itself

blocks.solution:
Use the output of the first application of f as a new input.

Substitute \(2 x + 7\) for x in \(f(x)\).

Final answer: \(4 x + 21\).
blocks.hint: Use the output of the first application of f as a new input.

retry.feedback: Composition applies the function again. Squaring the output gives a different expression.

sections.title: How can one rule limit the next?
sections.label: Restricted domain
sections.intro: An initial input can be allowed by the inner rule while the first output is refused by the outer rule.

blocks.html: Check both domains. Solve the condition that the first output fits the next rule's domain.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{x - 7}\) on its natural domain and \(g(x)=1 - 3 x\) for all real \(x\).

Find the domain of \(fg\).
blocks.solution:
The output of g must be a valid input of f.

Solve \(1 - 3 x\ge 7\). Reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number.

Final answer: \(x\le -2\).
blocks.hint: The output of g must be a valid input of f.

retry.feedback: Solve the condition on g(x), looking at the sign of its coefficient of x.

blocks.html: For an inverse inequality, dividing by a negative coefficient reverses the order.

blocks.solution:

Solve \(2 - 4 x\ge 7\). Reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number.

Final answer: \(x\le - \frac{5}{4}\).
blocks.hint: The output of g must be a valid input of f.

sections.title: How can I reverse a linear rule?

sections.intro: Write the original output as a new variable. Rearrange first, before giving the inverse its usual name.

blocks.html: Undo operations in reverse order.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=3 x + 4\), for real x.

Find \(f^{-1}(x)\).
blocks.solution:
Swap input and output, then isolate the new output.

Undo addition of \(4\), then undo multiplication by \(3\).

Final answer: \(\frac{x}{3} - \frac{4}{3}\).

sections.title: How can I undo a reciprocal rule?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: Move the output shift before multiplying by the denominator. This exposes the only prohibited inverse input.

blocks.html: A restriction on the original range becomes a restriction on the inverse domain.

blocks.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=4 + \frac{3}{x - 5}\), \(x\ne 5\).

Give the value excluded from the domain of the inverse.
blocks.solution:
Isolate the reciprocal term before switching the variable names.

From \(y=4 + \frac{3}{x - 5}\), multiply by \(x-5\) and divide by \(y-(4)\). The inverse excludes the original range gap. The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x)=5 + \frac{3}{x - 4}\).

Final answer: \(4\).
blocks.hint: Isolate the reciprocal term before switching the variable names.

blocks.html: A reciprocal shift in the output changes the denominator of the inverse.

blocks.prompt:

Final answer: \(-4\).

sections.title: Where does a point move on an inverse graph?
sections.label: Swap
sections.intro: For each plotted point, the first coordinate becomes the second coordinate and the second becomes the first.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.prompt:

Find the intersection of the line and its inverse.
blocks.solution:
Set the two line expressions equal. The common point is on the reflection line.

Use \(3 x + 5=x\) to find the fixed input \(- \frac{5}{2}\) and substitute it back.

Final answer: \((- \frac{5}{2},- \frac{5}{2})\).
